teach.title: It hangs a whole clause on a noun
teach.say: To say more about a noun than one adjective can, Latin hangs a small sentence on it with **the relative pronoun quī, quae, quod ('who, which, that')**, *prōnōmen relātīvum*: *puer quī rīdet* = the boy who is laughing. The noun in front is the antecedent, the word the clause is about; the clause has a verb of its own, so the sentence carries two verbs. Close the clause off at its verb and what is left over is the main sentence. The clause usually sits right after its noun, but it can also come after the main verb.

teach.title: The nominative: quī, quae, quod
teach.say: The pronoun looks back at its antecedent for two of its three labels, gender and number. When it is the subject of its own clause it stands in the nominative (the subject form): a masculine noun takes **quī**, a feminine one **quae**, a neuter one **quod** — *puer quī*, *puella quae*, *ōrnāmentum quod*. A plural noun in front gives a plural pronoun, and for the masculine that is **quī** again: *servī quī saccōs portant*.

teach.title: The accusative: the clause's own object
teach.say: The third label is decided inside the clause, not by the noun in front. If the pronoun is what that clause's verb acts on, it takes the accusative (the object form): masculine **quem**, feminine **quam**, neuter **quod**, and in the plural **quōs** and **quās** — *puella quam Mārcus pulsat*, the girl whom Marcus hits; *puellae quās Mārcus videt*. The antecedent is still the subject of the main sentence; only the pronoun's own case has moved.

teach.title: The odd pair: cuius and cui
teach.say: Two more cells break the pattern, and each of them is one form for every gender. The genitive (the owner form) is **cuius** = whose: *puella cuius māter cantat*, the girl whose mother is singing. The dative (the receiver form) is **cui** = to whom: *servus cui dominus nummōs dat*, the slave to whom the master gives coins. Learn them as a pair, exactly as *huius* and *huic* go together.

teach.title: After a preposition, and quibus
teach.say: The job left is the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form), the one a preposition takes: **quō** for masculine and neuter, **quā** for feminine — *taberna in quā gemmae sunt*, the shop in which the jewels are. In Latin the preposition comes first and the pronoun follows it. For more than one, the single form **quibus** does that job and the receiver's job as well: *puerī quibus Iūlius pira dat*, the boys to whom Julius gives pears.

teach.title: Asking, pointing, or linking?
teach.say: Three lookalikes share the same letters. *Quis?* asks a question and ends the sentence with a question mark. *Ille* points at a noun and adds no verb. *Quī* links, and it always drags a verb of its own along behind it: *quis est puer quī in viā plōrat?* — the first word asks, the second joins a clause. Find the extra verb and you have found the relative.

core.text: To add a whole clause about a noun, Latin uses **the relative pronoun qui, quae, quod ('who, which, that')**, *prōnōmen relātīvum*: *puer quī rīdet* = the boy who laughs; *puella quam Mārcus pulsat* = the girl whom Marcus hits. The noun it refers to (the antecedent) fixes its gender and number; its own job inside the clause fixes its case: *quī* (nominative) laughs, *quam* (accusative) gets hit.
A relative clause is the *who / which / that* part of *the man who is coming is my friend*. English still shows case in *who* (subject), *whom* (object) and *whose* (owner).
Gender and number from the noun before; case from the pronoun's own job in its clause. The odd forms: *cuius* (whose), *cui* (to whom), *quem* (whom), plural *quibus*.

invented.la: Servī quōs dominus vocat statim veniunt.
invented.en: The slaves whom the master calls come at once.

core.text: *Is* and *quī* share endings (*eum / quem*, *eī / cui*) and both point back to a noun, but *is* stays in its own sentence while *quī* opens a new clause with its own verb: *is servus* — that slave; *servus quī saccum portat* — the slave who carries the sack. A form of *quī* always has a verb of its own nearby.

more.text: From the learner's notes: the relative clause gives more information about its antecedent, and the pronoun's case is decided inside that clause — in *the woman whom he saw*, *whom* is the object of *saw*. The Latin forms mostly follow the -ius / -ī pattern of the demonstratives, with a few third-declension endings (*quem*, *quibus*). The notes' worked pairs: *vir … quī cibum comedit*, *fēmina … quae in hortō est*, *fēmina quam vir videt*, *fēminae quās*, *cuius pater fortis est*, *cui vir aquam fert*, *quibus*.

Ørberg cap. VIII lines the relative up with the question words *quis? quī? quem? cuius? cui? quō?* and with *is* / *ille*. A relative can open a sentence and refer back to the last one (*Quī …* = and he …). With no antecedent it means 'whoever, anyone who': *quī spīrat vīvus est* (r10:48.2). The neuter *quod* is also the conjunction 'because' (r10:23.1), and *in quā*, *ā quō* put the preposition before the pronoun (r08:1.1). A&G §303–307.
